title: 4 Team Motivation Drivers That Build Stakeholder Commitment 2026
author: Kurt Mueller
source: Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership (kurtmueller.substack.com), September 18,
summary: Kurt Mueller writes for newer leaders whose teams have already grasped that their job extends past their own silo to the stakeholders who depend on them, and who now face the predictable follow-up question of what is in it for me. His premise is that understanding the case for stakeholder commitment does not by itself generate the motivation to practice it, and that the tools which close that gap are cheap. He offers four. Make the contribution visible to the people whose opinions matter to that team member, because visibility links the behavior to reputation and career opportunity rather than to private thanks. Celebrate the behavior specifically, naming what someone actually did, since recognition only teaches the rest of the team when they can see what earned it. Recognize the attempt and not just the win, which Mueller calls the most overlooked driver, because a team that is praised only for flawless outcomes stops experimenting. Finally, convert demonstrated judgment into real ownership by handing over more discretion and influence. He closes by asking the reader to pick the single driver their team most needs and use it the next time the situation arises.
points: Mueller treats the question what is in it for me as legitimate rather than selfish, since cross-functional ownership asks people to change habits, priorities and their own definition of success.
Making a contribution visible to people whose opinion matters to that team member is the first driver, because visibility ties the behavior to reputation, credibility and career opportunity.
Recognition works as instruction only when the specific action is named, so a staff meeting shout-out should describe what two people actually did instead of saying great job.
The most overlooked driver is recognizing the attempt: if only flawless outcomes earn praise, people learn to stop experimenting with difficult cross-functional relationships.
The fourth driver converts demonstrated stakeholder judgment into more discretion and influence, so good behavior leads to real ownership rather than only to praise.
quotes: They understand that their job is not simply to complete their part of the work. They also have a responsibility to help solve problems for the stakeholders who depend on them.
That isn’t necessarily selfish. You are asking people to change habits, priorities, and sometimes even how they define success.
Understanding the need for stakeholder commitment does not automatically create the motivation to practice it.
Why? Because visibility connects the desired behavior with reputation, credibility, and career opportunity.
The important part is identifying what they did, not simply saying, “Great job.
If people are only recognized when everything works perfectly, they quickly learn to avoid experimentation.
When a team meber demonstrates good stakeholder judgment, give them a little more responsibility, discretion, or influence.

Stakeholder commitment rarely comes from telling people, “We need to collaborate more.” It develops when your team discovers that stakeholder-focused behavior leads to recognition, visibility, future opportunites, and greater trust.
